hook: For adults with ADHD, the phone alert meant to pull them back to work is often the thing that pulls them further away.
lede: In the survey that opens this thesis, 93.3% of adults with ADHD said their minds wander most in meetings or classes: exactly the rooms where a chime draws stares and a glowing screen invites a second distraction. Capace takes another route. It is an ordinary black baseball cap that reads two channels of forehead EEG and answers a drifting mind with touch, a knock, a pulse or a slow sweep around the head that only the wearer can feel. This thesis follows it from 124 survey responses to a working prototype tested with 24 adults with ADHD.

chapters.title: A day that slips away in pieces
paragraphs: The thesis first draws the problem as a day, through a persona built from interviews and a 30-day focus group: a 27-year-old product manager diagnosed in childhood. She delays getting up by scrolling her phone, drifts between her desk and the pantry, and a few minutes into the morning meeting looks attentive while her mind wanders off.

Her afternoon swings between extremes. After lunch her brain seems to shut down; then tasks flood in, and under pressure she can tip into hyperfocus, working for hours, refusing every interruption and forgetting to rest. Late at night, still scrolling, she recalls everything left undone and goes to sleep after a round of harsh self-criticism.

The diaries behind her are blunt. Over three weeks, most participants reported that their attention fell off a cliff after 1 p.m. and again after 10 p.m., and that once a task derailed it was very hard to get back on track. To-do lists helped in the morning; by night, the unfinished items set off self-blame.

chapters.title: Help that interrupts, distracts and stares back
paragraphs: Existing aids, mostly phone apps and wrist-worn devices, fail that day in three ways. Fixed-interval buzzes ignore what the wearer is doing, breaking deep focus until the brain learns to tune them out. Screens and chimes overload easily flooded senses, and lighting up a phone to check a reminder puts social apps one glance away. A medical-looking headset, or a device that beeps in a quiet meeting room, invites stigma.

The survey pointed elsewhere. Respondents favored the head (83.7%) as a wearing position and vibration (79.6%) as the feedback channel, while ringing alerts drew 35 outright “reverse” votes in a KANO analysis. In the focus group, people asked for AI that could “explain itself clearly, and be switched off”.

chapters.title: Eight sensations the body already knows
paragraphs: A notification is a symbol that must be noticed, decoded and understood, adding load to a mind already struggling. Drawing on embodied cognition, Capace speaks instead in touches borrowed from everyday physical experience. Eight small actuators ring the head, so a cue can come from one direction, fire all at once, or seem to travel across the scalp.

Three parameters shape every cue. Waveform sets arousal: sharp pulses wake, smooth waves soothe. Timing sets rhythm: irregular bursts break “sticky” states, steady rhythms guide. Location sets scope: a single point is a directional anchor, the full array a global sensation. Combined, they give eight patterns, one for each attention difficulty the research identified:
points: Mind-wandering: a knock on the head, two crisp taps like a teacher’s tap on the forehead
Hyperfocus: thunder, irregular and intense bursts from three random points
Procrastination: a ringing clock, two side actuators building over 10 seconds
Trouble switching tasks: a button press, all eight actuators firing once together
Misplaced objects: a compass, a gentle steady buzz from the target’s direction
Sensory overload: a shield, soft synchronized pulses like tactile white noise
Cognitive fatigue: temple kneading, the two temple actuators alternating smoothly
Emotional instability: a deep breath, a wave that circles the head for 4 s, rests 7 s and circles back for 8 s

figures.caption: The eight patterns (a–h): which actuators fire, and each actuator’s signal over time.

chapters.title: One signal, read in context
paragraphs: Two forehead electrodes cannot reliably tell eight states apart, and a device that buzzes at the wrong moment can push easily frustrated users to abandon it. So the brain signal is asked only one question: focused or drifting? A multi-band EEGNet-GRU splits each 3-second window from FP1 and FP2 into five frequency bands and follows how each unfolds over time. Pretrained on a public dataset cut down from 64 channels to these two, it reached 81.1% accuracy and caught 82.9% of mind-wandering windows, where a support vector machine caught only 30.1%.

Context supplies the rest, with the system acting as what the thesis calls an “external prefrontal” node. A decision tree combines the drift probability with the task state, so the same number changes meaning: high during an active task, it means mind-wandering and triggers the knock; high after a task was due to start, it signals procrastination and sets off the clock; very low once a task has overrun, it means hyperfocus and brings the thunder. Sensory overload, emotional distress and misplaced objects are left to the user, one button away in the app.

figures.caption: The multi-band EEGNet-GRU: one convolutional branch and GRU per frequency band, combined for classification.

chapters.title: A lab hidden in a baseball cap
paragraphs: Guided by calm technology, the thesis weighed six head-worn forms. Headbands and hair accessories read as sports gear or EEG tests, masks and crowns are too theatrical; the classic baseball cap is common, roomy and able to hide everything inside.

A 3D-printed TPU “octopus” skeleton reaches out from the crown to hold the eight actuators against the head, and a mesh liner covers everything except the electrodes. At the back sit the OpenBCI board, an ESP32 controller and a 2000 mAh battery whose weight balances the front. From the outside, as participant M18 later put it, “No one can tell you’re using a special device.”

The companion app answers the night-time self-blame the diaries revealed. Review pages chart attention in neutral shades instead of red “failure” marks, and an LLM assistant looks for moments of resilience in the user’s own data, even on days when tasks went unfinished.

chapters.title: What happened when 24 adults put it on
paragraphs: Twenty-four adults with diagnosed ADHD spent about two hours with Capace. Given no hints, they matched the eight vibrations to their meanings 42.5% of the time, against 12.5% chance; after a brief explanation, accuracy rose to 76.8% (p < 0.001).

In a sustained-attention task (SART), a knock after each error lowered the average number of errors from 2.42 to 1.45, while responses slowed slightly, from 412.6 to 435.2 ms: a speed–accuracy trade-off. In a search task, a compass cue from the target’s direction cut completion time from 3315.8 to 2450.3 ms (p < 0.001). And applied directly to 146 mind-wandering segments recorded during the SART, the pretrained detector was right 83.61% of the time.

Ten participants then wore the cap for 60 minutes on their own tasks. All six user-experience dimensions scored above 3.5 out of 5, led by novelty (4.52), which may partly reflect a novelty effect; perspicuity was lowest (3.85), since eight patterns are a lot to learn.

Crisp, strong cues such as the clock and the knock won praise; temple kneading was sometimes easy to ignore, and thick hair dulled the vibrations. F7 admitted, “At first I felt like I was being controlled by the cap.” The thunder that F3 said could jolt them out of hyperfocus struck F1 as merely startling and uncomfortable.

quote.text: If it’s too strong, it completely breaks my train of thought; if it’s too weak, I just ignore it.

takeaways: Attention support can move off the screen: a private touch on the head avoids the second distraction and the stigma that chimes and screens bring.
Minimal sensing goes further with context: two forehead channels plus the task state can separate difficulties the signal alone cannot.
Bodily metaphors make a haptic vocabulary quick to learn, but eight cues are a lot; the thesis suggests letting each user pick a few core patterns and testing them in everyday life.
